name: How to Compare ADU Addition Contractor Bids in Los Angeles County

mainEntity.name: How should I compare bids from ADU additions contractors in Los Angeles County so I don’t underbudget for structural and utility upgrades?
mainEntity.text: How should I compare bids from ADU additions contractors in Los Angeles County so I don’t underbudget for structural and utility upgrades?

acceptedAnswer.text: Comparing bids for an ADU addition in Los Angeles County is challenging because contractors structure proposals differently. Start by requesting detailed, itemized estimates from each ADU additions contractor, separating design, permits, structural engineering, demolition, framing, utilities, finishes, and site work. Confirm whether utility upgrades—such as panel increases, sewer line replacement, or water service upsizing—are a fixed price, allowance, or excluded item. Ask if structural engineering fees and any special reports (like soils, if needed) are included. Review whether the contractor has budgeted for plan check corrections, not just the initial submittal, since revisions are common. Look closely at allowances for finishes such as cabinets, tile, and flooring; unrealistically low allowances make a bid appear cheaper but drive change orders later. Request that each contractor identify specific contingencies for hidden conditions in existing walls, roofs, and foundations, and how they will price and approve those discoveries with you. A clear exclusions list is critical: you want to know exactly what is not covered. When you line up bids with comparable scopes and assumptions, you can see whether one is genuinely more efficient or simply incomplete. Choosing based solely on the lowest headline number is a common cause of budget overruns on ADU additions.
acceptedAnswer.description: To compare ADU additions contractor bids accurately, line up each scope and confirm whether structural engineering, utility upgrades, plan check corrections, and contingencies for hidden conditions are included. Beware low bids that omit design, permit, or upgrade allowances, as these often lead to large change orders later.
